solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Do gaffes regularly? They may

indicators.note: something done regularly happens at even intervals, so every second letter of the phrase is kept

parts.note: the even-placed letters of the two words

explanation.surface: A question about whether someone commits blunders as a habit, with the reply that certain people may.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is the definition: clumsy louts are just the people who might make gaffes regularly.
explanation.definitionFit: Oafs are clumsy, tactless people, the sort expected to commit social blunders.

clue.text: They may take back issues on board

definitions.text: They may take back issues on board

parts.note: surface reading: people who accept old magazine numbers, or editors absorbing returned copies
setter's reading: problems with the spine, which these practitioners take on as patients

explanation.walkthrough: Back issues suggests old copies of a magazine; here it means spinal complaints, and to take on board is to accept as work.
explanation.definitionFit: These practitioners treat musculoskeletal problems, especially of the spine, by manipulating the body.

clue.text: French gentlemen stopping payment for a Parisienne?

indicators.note: to stop something is to plug it, so one piece sits inside the other like a stopper

parts.note: a fee is a payment for a service
MM is the abbreviation for messieurs, French for gentlemen

explanation.surface: French gentlemen refusing to pay for a woman from Paris.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags that the definition is a French word: a Parisienne is a woman, and the French for woman is the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Femme is the French word for woman, so it names a Parisienne by example.

clue.text: Ready to absorb large amount in real business

indicators.note: what absorbs something takes it inside itself, so one piece goes within the other

parts.note: ready and brass are both British slang for cash
a stack is a large quantity, as in stacks of money

explanation.surface: Cash on hand soaking up a big sum in a genuine commercial venture.
explanation.walkthrough: Ready (as in ready money) and brass are both British slang for cash; the five-letter heap sits between the fourth and fifth letters of the money.
explanation.definitionFit: Getting down to brass tacks is an idiom for dealing with the essential, practical facts of a matter.

clue.text: Quiet activity in southern English town

definitions.meaning: first meaning: looking through a book, a silent pastime
second meaning: a large town in Berkshire, west of London

explanation.surface: Someone enjoying a peaceful pursuit in a town in the south of England.
explanation.walkthrough: The town is spelt like the activity but said with a short e, as 'redding'.
explanation.definitionFit: The everyday pastime of perusing a book shares its spelling with the Berkshire town.

clue.text: Starry McCartney's "Back in the USSR"

parts.note: Stella McCartney is a fashion designer, daughter of Paul

indicators.note: the back of a word is its end, so only the closing letter of that phrase is used

parts.note: the final letter of the phrase

explanation.surface: A rave review of Paul McCartney's Beatles song Back in the USSR.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface makes McCartney Paul and the song title a title; the setter means his daughter Stella and the end of the last word.
explanation.definitionFit: Stellar describes anything relating to the stars, so it is a synonym of starry.

clue.text: Clipped recording shows a soft goal

indicators.note: something clipped has had its end trimmed off, so the last letter goes

parts.note: taping is recording on tape

explanation.surface: A shortened video replay showing an easy score in a football match.
explanation.definitionFit: In football a tap-in is an easy goal, gently pushed over the line from very close range.

clue.text: Funny fellow touring does broadcast? The end of it

indicators.note: to broadcast seed is to scatter it, so these letters are thrown into a new order
one touring a place goes all round it, so this piece wraps round the other

parts.note: a clown is a comic performer
the four letters rearranged

explanation.surface: A comedian on tour does a broadcast, and asks what happens at the end of it.
explanation.walkthrough: Broadcast and the end of it look like one surface thought; the first scrambles a word and the second defines the station signing off for the night.
explanation.definitionFit: A closedown is the end of a day's transmissions by a radio or television station.

clue.text: Type of gin measured by the sound of it

indicators.note: judging by how a word sounds means the spoken form counts, not its spelling

parts.note: measured, as in a measured pace, means unhurried

explanation.surface: A question of the kind of gin poured by the measure.
explanation.walkthrough: Measured looks like a reference to pub measures of gin; it means deliberate and unhurried.
explanation.definitionFit: Sloe gin is a liqueur made by steeping blackthorn berries in gin.

clue.text: Element found in a state

indicators.note: to found metal is to melt and cast it, so these letters are recast into a new shape

parts.note: all eight letters rearranged

explanation.surface: A chemical element discovered within one of the American states.
explanation.walkthrough: In a state looks like an anagram signal or a location; it is the fodder, and found is the signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Astatine is a rare radioactive chemical element, a halogen with atomic number 85.

clue.text: Newspaper run briskly in temporary accommodation

parts.note: The Times is a newspaper, the setter's own paper's sister
to hare is to run very fast

explanation.surface: A newspaper being run in a hurry from some temporary lodgings.
explanation.definitionFit: A timeshare is a holiday property owned jointly, each owner using it for set weeks of the year.

clue.text: Publicity for short period of time?

parts.note: pro means in favour of, as in pros and cons
mo is short for moment

explanation.surface: Asking whether publicity is meant for only a brief spell.
explanation.walkthrough: Short looks like it describes the period; it marks the time word as abbreviated.
explanation.definitionFit: A promo is a promotional piece, such as a trailer or advert, used to publicise something.

clue.text: Patience, for example, Met show?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: Patience is a Gilbert and Sullivan comic work for the stage
second meaning: what the Metropolitan ... House in New York puts on

explanation.surface: Asking whether forbearance was shown when two people met.
explanation.walkthrough: Patience looks like the virtue and Met like the past of meet; one is a Gilbert and Sullivan title and the other New York's opera house.
explanation.definitionFit: Patience is a Gilbert and Sullivan comic work, and the Met in New York stages musical dramas of that kind.

clue.text: Friendly person is one getting abuse

parts.note: the Roman numeral for one
slander is spoken defamation, verbal abuse

explanation.surface: A kindly person turns out to be the one on the receiving end of insults.
explanation.walkthrough: Friendly takes a capital here: Tonga is known as the Friendly Islands, so a Friendly person is someone from there.
explanation.definitionFit: An inhabitant of an island group such as the Friendly Islands is called an islander.

clue.text: Conversation of old gipsies not working

indicators.note: something not working is out of order, so these letters are out of their order

parts.note: all ten letters rearranged

explanation.surface: The talk of elderly travellers with nothing to do.
explanation.definitionFit: Idle gossip is casual chatter about other people, a kind of conversation with no serious purpose.

clue.text: Humiliating offence breaks one ugly woman

parts.note: a means one

indicators.note: something that breaks into a thing gets inside it, so this piece goes within the other

parts.note: bag is a derogatory slang term for an unattractive woman
a sin is a moral offence

explanation.surface: A crime that ruins a plain-looking woman is degrading.
explanation.definitionFit: Abasing means lowering someone in dignity or esteem, which is humiliating them.

clue.text: Chief financial backer in Russian port

parts.note: arch means principal, as in archenemy
an angel is an investor, especially in a theatre production

explanation.surface: The main investor based in a Russian harbour city.
explanation.definitionFit: Arkhangelsk, called Archangel in English, is a port city on the White Sea in northern Russia.

clue.text: Conservative MP, big in California?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: John ..., long-serving Conservative member of the UK parliament
second meaning: the giant tree that grows on the Californian coast

explanation.surface: Asking whether a British Tory politician is famous in California.
explanation.walkthrough: Big in California reads as famous there; it means physically huge, describing a tree.
explanation.definitionFit: John Redwood is a Conservative politician, and the coast redwood is California's enormous native conifer.

clue.text: Unproductive time lost in eg Dakar, capital of Senegal

indicators.note: something lost has wandered off course, so these letters stray from their order

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: the capital of a word is its opening letter, so only that is kept

parts.note: the opening letter

explanation.surface: A spell of time wasted in the Senegalese capital, Dakar.
explanation.walkthrough: Dakar really is the capital of Senegal, which makes capital of Senegal look like a description; it supplies only one letter.
explanation.definitionFit: The Dark Ages, figuratively, is any period of stagnation or lack of progress, from the early medieval era.

clue.text: Hot money for cybercriminals

parts.note: H is the abbreviation for hot, as on taps
ackers is British slang for money

explanation.surface: Stolen cash ending up with online crooks.
explanation.walkthrough: Hot money suggests stolen funds; the words are taken separately, and ackers is old British slang for cash.
explanation.definitionFit: Hackers break into computer systems without permission, which makes them online criminals.

clue.text: It's clear your setter's head over heels in love!

indicators.note: turning head over heels flips something end to end, so the letters run backwards

parts.note: net, as in net profit, means clear after deductions
the setter is Tim Moorey, so his name with the possessive

explanation.surface: The setter openly confesses to being madly in love.
explanation.walkthrough: Head over heels in love reads as one phrase meaning the answer, but the first part flips the letters; your setter is Tim Moorey.
explanation.definitionFit: Smitten means struck by sudden infatuation, strongly attracted to someone.

clue.text: Inflamed swelling, temperature dropping? Call for injection with this

indicators.note: an injection puts something inside, so this piece is pushed into the other
something dropping falls away, so the named letter leaves the word

parts.note: a stye is an inflamed swelling on the eyelid
T is the abbreviation for temperature
to ring is to phone

explanation.surface: Advice to a patient with a fevered swelling: once the temperature falls, ask for a jab.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is the final pair of words, read with injection before them: you give an injection with this. Without its T the swelling becomes SYE.
explanation.definitionFit: A syringe is the tube and needle a medical injection is given with.

clue.text: Poland in current upturn spend extravagantly

indicators.note: in places one piece inside the other, plainly

parts.note: a surge is a sudden rise, as of electric current or in the economy
PL is the international code for Poland

explanation.surface: Poles, buoyed by an economic upswing, start splashing out.
explanation.walkthrough: Upturn looks like a reversal signal; it is part of the definition of a sudden rise.
explanation.definitionFit: To splurge is to spend money freely and lavishly on luxuries.

clue.text: Fellow's training a monkey in Africa

parts.note: a man is a fellow
drill is repetitive training, as of soldiers

explanation.surface: A man is teaching an African monkey.
explanation.definitionFit: The mandrill is a large West African primate with a brightly coloured face, related to the baboons.

clue.text: Mentioned stupid reductions in size

indicators.note: something mentioned is spoken, so the word is heard, not seen

parts.note: dense means slow-witted

explanation.surface: Someone referred to foolish cuts in scale.
explanation.definitionFit: Dents are reductions, as when a large bill makes a dent in savings.

clue.text: Trouble since Greece brought in

indicators.note: what is brought in is taken inside, so one piece sits within the other

parts.note: ago means back in time, as in long since
GR is the abbreviation for Greece

explanation.surface: Difficulties ever since Greece joined.
explanation.walkthrough: Aggro is British slang for aggressive trouble-making.
explanation.definitionFit: Aggro, short for aggravation, is informal British for hostile behaviour or bother.

clue.text: Old boring taste in a French restaurant? Leave

indicators.note: something boring drills into another thing, so this piece goes inside

parts.note: gout, written goût, is French for taste
O is the abbreviation for old

explanation.surface: A dull dish in a French bistro, so walk out.
explanation.walkthrough: Boring looks like it describes the taste; it means drilling into.
explanation.definitionFit: To go out is to leave a room or building.

clue.text: Henry with head for figures gets one over a couple

parts.note: Hal is a pet name for Henry, as in Shakespeare's Prince Hal

indicators.note: the head of a word is its first letter, so only that is kept

parts.note: the opening letter

explanation.surface: Henry, who is good with numbers, scores one over par in a pair.
explanation.walkthrough: One over a couple is read as a fraction: one on top of two.
explanation.definitionFit: A half is the fraction one over two, written 1/2.

clue.text: Gas man finally following a right turn

parts.note: taken as written
R is the abbreviation for right
a go is a turn in a game

indicators.note: finally points to the end, so only the closing letter of that word is kept

parts.note: the final letter

explanation.surface: A gas fitter finally turns right.
explanation.walkthrough: Right turn reads as a direction on the road; turn is a go, as in whose go is it.
explanation.definitionFit: Argon is a noble gas, the third most common in the air we breathe.

clue.text: Hill exercise is sufficient for wrecks!

parts.note: a tor is a rocky hill, as on Dartmoor
PE is physical education
that does means that will be enough

explanation.surface: Hill walking is enough to ruin someone.
explanation.definitionFit: To torpedo something is to destroy or sabotage it, so the verb means wrecks.

clue.text: Entertainer has relations in Germany

parts.note: folks are one's family
taken as written
GER is the abbreviation for Germany

explanation.surface: A performer has family living in Germany.
explanation.definitionFit: A folk singer performs traditional songs, a kind of entertainer.

clue.text: Queue's said to follow this series at peaks

definitions.text: Queue's said to follow this series
definitions.meaning: first meaning: the run of the alphabet from A as far as P, which the letter pronounced like queue comes after
second meaning: on top of, at the summit

explanation.walkthrough: Read the answer as A TO P: the letter Q, said like queue, follows that stretch of the alphabet.
explanation.definitionFit: Atop is a preposition meaning on the top of, so things atop the hills are at peaks.
